title: Guard /settings writes by provenance
wave: M4 Wave B (shippable: false — merges with M4-4, one review, one changelog gate)
one_line: When you change a setting in the /settings panel but a project config, a --config overlay, a runtime override, or an environment variable still supplies the effective value, the panel now says which layer is shadowing it and the dead value never gets written to your global config.
user_visible_effect: Turning on a setting that a project's .omp/config.yml already sets no longer silently writes a dead duplicate into the global config.yml and calls it 'applied' — the row reports which layer is overriding the panel value instead. Same for an env var (already partly reported today), a --config/PI_CONFIG_FILES overlay, and a runtime override. Settings that are NOT shadowed behave exactly as before, so /settings is not bricked for anyone.

steps.instruction: Create packages/coding-agent/src/config/shadowing.ts. Move `globalValue` (config-cli.ts:318-322) into it renamed `globalLayerValue`, and `shadowingSource` (config-cli.ts:325-360) into it unchanged in body. Give BOTH an explicit `scope: Settings` parameter instead of closing over the `settings` module proxy — `globalLayerValue` reads `scope.getGlobalSettings()` and `shadowingSource` calls `setting.provenance(scope)`. Export `SettingProvenance` as a re-export of the type from ./settings so callers of the new module do not need a second import. Keep the exact same message strings — the CLI output is user-facing and already shipped.

In config-cli.ts delete both local functions and add a top-level `import { globalLayerValue, shadowingSource } from "../config/shadowing";`. Update the two call sites inside handleSet (currently line 307) to pass `settings` as the second/third argument. Verify `bun run check:ts` is still clean — this is a pure move, so any error here means the extraction was not faithful.

In settings-defs.ts, immediately above the `SettingsHost` interface, add `export type SettingsProvenance = "env" | "runtime" | "overlay" | "project" | "global" | "default";` and add `provenance(path: string): SettingsProvenance;` to the interface with a doc comment explaining the ordering: runtime override -> --config overlay -> project -> global -> schema default, with env checked first and therefore only reachable through this method.

In settings-ui.ts widen `set` to return a result. Define and export `SettingsWriteResult` as a discriminated union: `{ status: "applied" } | { status: "shadowed"; source: Exclude<SettingsProvenance, "global" | "default">; message: string }`. Note that the narrow `source` type is the point of the change — it makes the rollback branch and the UI branch exhaustive.

Implement the guard in `createSettingsHost`'s `set` (line 77). Four steps, in this exact order: (1) `const previous = globalLayerValue(setting, settings);` — undefined means the key was absent from the global layer; (2) `setting.set(settings, value);`; (3) read back what actually landed normalised via `const written = globalLayerValue(setting, settings);` and the effective value via `const effective = setting.get(settings);`, then `const shadow = shadowingSource(setting, settings);` — (4) early-return `{ status: "applied" }` when `shadow` is undefined OR when `Bun.deepEquals(effective, written)`, because a higher layer holding the identical value is not a real shadow. Otherwise roll back: `previous === undefined ? setting.unset(settings) : setting.set(settings, previous);` and return `{ status: "shadowed", source: shadow source, message: shadow.message }`.

Add `provenance: path => resolve(path).provenance(settings)` to the host object literal. The declared return type of `SettingsHost.provenance` is what enforces the mirror: if coding-agent's `SettingProvenance` ever gains a member, this arrow function stops type-checking and `bun run check:ts` goes red. That is the drift guard — do not add a runtime assertion on top of it.

In settings-selector.ts add a private `#writeSetting(path: string, value: unknown): boolean` to SettingsSelectorComponent that calls `this.#context.settings.set(path, value)`, and on `status === "shadowed"` shows `message` through whatever inline error/status affordance the component already has, returning false; otherwise returning true. Then replace all 13 call sites — lines 349, 393, 876, 879, 1162, 1200, 1202, 1216, 1218, 1220, 1222, 1251, 1258 — with `#writeSetting(...)`.

For the two ProviderLimitsSubmenu sites (349 and 393) note that `this.#settings` is a separate SettingsHost field on that class, not `this.#context.settings` — the helper either takes the host as a parameter or is duplicated once on ProviderLimitsSubmenu. Pick one; do not silently drop those two writes, they are the record-setting path and the easiest to miss.
Run `grep -c 'settings\.set(' packages/tui/src/overlays/settings-selector.ts` — it must now print 0. Any non-zero value means step 7 missed a site and the guard has a hole.

Generalise `envNote` (settings-ui.ts:39-44) into a `provenanceNote(setting)` that appends to the description for every shadowing layer, not just env, reusing the lifted `shadowingSource` message strings so the panel and `omp config set` say the same words. This is what makes the shadow visible BEFORE the user writes, and it is the fix for the gap the plan names. Keep envNote's existing env-specific wording for the env case — it is already shipped and users recognise it.
Write packages/coding-agent/test/config/settings-provenance-guard.test.ts — see test_contract below for the six cases and the exact fixtures.

Do NOT add a changelog entry. Wave B is `shippable: false` (plan line 7925) and is gated behind a single M4 changelog decision that has not been made. Both packages' `[Unreleased]` sections stay untouched. Note the shape of this change in the PR body instead.

test_contract: The observable contract: a /settings write whose effective value is supplied by a higher layer must (a) not leave the dead value in the global config.yml on disk, (b) leave the setting's previous global value exactly as it was, and (c) report which layer is shadowing. A write with nothing shadowing it must land normally in config.yml. If the guard regresses, a user toggles a setting that their project config already controls and config.yml silently accumulates dead values that appear applied — the exact failure M4-6 exists to prevent. The no-shadow control row is not filler: it is what proves the guard distinguishes 'shadowed' from 'applied', and it is the test that fails if someone turns the guard into a blanket refusal and bricks /settings for every user (the risk the plan names as the primary failure mode).

gate:
Four gates, all mechanical and all able to go red.
(1) `grep -c 'settings\.set(' packages/tui/src/overlays/settings-selector.ts` prints 0 — no write bypasses the guard. This is the anti-drift gate: it goes red the moment anyone adds a 14th call site the way the plan's hardcoded line list would have silently missed.
(2) The project-shadow test asserts `YAML.parse(await Bun.file(globalConfigPath).text())` does NOT contain the key after a panel write, and that it contains the PRE-write value — a byte-level assertion on the real file, which is what rollback means here (in-memory revert before the 100ms `#queueSave` debounce drains, so the write and its rollback coalesce into one save; verified settings.ts:818-838 and #queueSave).
(3) The no-shadow control test asserts the same key IS present in config.yml after a panel write with nothing shadowing it. Without this, gates (1) and (2) are satisfiable by a guard that refuses every write.
(4) `bun run check:ts` clean, which additionally enforces that tui's `SettingsProvenance` and coding-agent's `SettingProvenance` have not drifted.

risk: The guard is a post-write verification with rollback, and the rollback decision is what can brick /settings. Two concrete ways this goes wrong. (1) A blanket refusal — if the guard rejects every write whose provenance is not "global", then for any setting a project config already defines, the panel becomes read-only and users cannot edit it at all. The no-shadow control test exists specifically to catch this, and the guard must be value-comparing (effective vs written) rather than provenance-only, because a project layer holding the identical value is a false positive. (2) A throw escaping the guard — none of the 13 call sites is wrapped in try/catch (confirmed: the only `throw` in settings-selector.ts is the two `Invalid record JSON` throws at lines 1208 and 1211), so a thrown error from `set` propagates into the component's submit handler and can take down the overlay mid-render. The guard must RETURN a result, never throw for shadowing; genuine write failures (bad JSON, validation) still throw as they do today. Secondary risk, lower: the tui/coding-agent interface drift — `SettingsHost` is declared in tui and satisfied structurally by `createSettingsHost` in coding-agent, and packages/tui/package.json exports `./*` as a wildcard, so out-of-repo implementors exist in principle. Adding one member is far less dangerous than M4-4's return-type change, but the wildcard export is why the provenance member must be additive and optional-free rather than a signature change.
open_questions: Should the panel be LOUD or QUIET on a shadowed write? The spec returns a result and the panel shows an inline message. But a user who typed a value into a text field and pressed enter, and then sees it silently revert, may read that as data loss. Options: (a) reject the write and show why, (b) allow the write, keep it in config.yml, and only annotate the row. Option (b) is what `omp config set` already does today (config-cli.ts:315-317 — it reports the shadow in yellow and leaves the value written), so it has shipped precedent; option (a) is what the dsh precedent did. This is a product decision, not an engineering one, and it changes whether the rollback half of the guard exists at all.

The plan's dsh precedent (`packages/boot/config-editor/src/index.ts:127-129` and `:133-137`) DOES NOT EXIST in this repo — there is no `packages/boot/` package at all. The rollback-by-bytes half of the plan's design therefore rests on precedent that cannot be inspected here. The in-repo precedent is config-cli.ts:295-318, which verifies post-write but reports rather than rolls back. Decide which precedent governs before writing the guard.

Should `provenanceNote` (step 10) be applied to the settings' persistent description, or only shown after a write? A persistent description note is strictly more informative and costs nothing, but it changes the description of every shadowed row, which is a wider visual change than the plan scoped. It also grows the entry list, which is rebuilt on every tab switch (`#buildItemsForDefs` at settings-selector.ts:1280) — cheap, but worth confirming with a real settings count.

Confirm the M2 WI-8a / WI-8b dependency has actually landed. The plan states it as a hard blocker but M2 has not been executed; if those items changed the settings-registration surface, step 3's interface addition may need to match a shape that does not exist yet.
